transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-01-27
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Aisha (Foxglove VP Eng), Tom (Cloud Architect), Joan (Security), Paul (NetOps)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be rough): Quick intake on network topology; customer requires EU-only model with private endpoints; concerned about egress and audit logs; next: diagram + security pack + pilot pricing.

-- Transcript --
[00:00:05] Lena: Hey everyone, uh thanks for joining, I'm Lena with Redwood, and with me are Marcus and Priya from our solutions engineering team. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:14] Aisha: Good, thanks. Running a bit late earlier but all good now.
[00:00:18] Tom: Yep, thanks for coordinating. We got Paul's calendar freed up so happy to deep dive.
[00:00:23] Lena: Great. The goal here is to understand your networking constraints and regional gating so we can map out a private deployment path. Marcus, do you want to kick off?
[00:00:31] Marcus: Sure. Uh quick agenda — we'll ask about current cloud footprint, network topology, security reqs, then talk options: private endpoints in each region, VPC peering, or hub transit gateway approach. We'll also cover failover and what hosted fallback would look like.
[00:00:48] Joan: Just to flag up front — Foxglove is under EU data residency for product logs and certain PII. So any traffic or storage for those datasets must stay in eu-west-1 or eu-central-1.
[00:00:59] Priya: Got it. Do you have a preferred region today?
[00:01:03] Aisha: eu-west-1 is primary, eu-central-1 is DR. We avoid US regions for model inferencing with PII.
[00:01:10] Marcus: That maps fine to our Private offering. One quick question on network topology — are you using a hub-and-spoke model with a transit gateway or is it direct peering between VPCs?
[00:01:21] Paul: We run TGW for core services, yeah. But a lot of teams still use direct peer for low-latency paths.
[00:01:28] Tom: We also have a dedicated firewall stack in the hub that inspects egress and enforces egress allow-lists.
[00:01:34] Marcus: OK perfect. For Redwood Private we can either attach via VPC peering straight into the customer's application VPCs, or create private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) in your account and route through the TGW. Peering is simpler but at scale the hub model is easier to manage.
[00:01:49] Tom: Can you explain the tradeoffs again? I heard "peering is simpler" but what's the operational difference?
[00:01:54] Marcus: Sure — peering is a point-to-point route, low overhead, but you need N peering relationships if you have N VPCs. With TGW, you have a central route table and the Redwood Private endpoint can be attached as a spoke, and policies flow through the hub. Also egress inspection remains centralized.
[00:02:10] Joan: About egress — our compliance team requires that all outbound traffic to third-party model repos be filtered and logged. If Redwood has egress that initiates external calls, how do we ensure those are blocked or inspected?
[00:02:21] Priya: On Private we don't initiate third-party model fetches from your environment — we serve models from the runtime you host. But there are background metrics/ops endpoints; we can route telemetry to an internal collector or disable telemetry.
[00:02:34] Lena: Also we support network egress policies where you can pin endpoints and outbound IP ranges; we can present those to your firewall team for allow-listing or block everything by default.
[00:02:43] Aisha: Good. One of our other concerns is key management — we use AWS KMS with external key material (XKM) for certain keys. Does Redwood integrate with customer-managed KMS?
[00:02:54] Priya: Yes, we support customer KMS for encryption at rest and can integrate with your KMS via IAM roles. HSM-backed keys are something we can discuss for higher-tier Private installs; that may need an architecture review.
[00:03:07] Paul: If we do PrivateLink endpoints, do those sit in our account or do they live in Redwood's account?
[00:03:13] Marcus: They usually live in your account — we deploy endpoint services from the Private control plane into a connector VPC and you accept them, but we can also do cross-account attachments depending on filesystem and IAM controls. There are a couple of models, we'll share the runbook.
[00:03:27] Tom: We have some teams that need ultra-low latency for real-time inference (sub-50ms). Do you have benchmarks for latency in-region versus cross-region?
[00:03:37] Marcus: We have internal profiles. Single-token tail-latency depends on model size, hardware, and KV cache hits. In-region with dedicated GPUs we see sub-20ms for small models, 50-100ms for large LLMs. Cross-region will add network RTT; eu->us would kill latency for you so we'll avoid that per your residency note.
[00:03:54] Aisha: Understood. We also need to know about DNS and internal naming — will the service be accessible via private DNS in our VPC?
[00:04:02] Priya: Yes, we can publish private DNS entries into your VPC resolver for endpoint endpoints so code can call a standard host. Sometimes we see issues with split-horizon DNS; we'll include guidance.
[00:04:13] Joan: Audit logs — do you ship logs to our S3 buckets or can we pull them? We need a tamper-evident trail.
[00:04:20] Marcus: We can forward audit logs to your S3 or publish to a logging endpoint in your tenancy. We also support syslog/CloudWatch exports and can do signed log delivery. We'll include log retention options in the package.
[00:04:31] Tom: Any special IP planning needs? Our IP space is tight.
[00:04:34] Marcus: We'll ask for VPC CIDRs. For peering we just need non-overlapping CIDRs. For TGW attachments there are route propagation concerns but that can be worked. We'll send a template.
[00:04:45] Paul: What about IAM — do you require cross-account roles?
[00:04:48] Priya: We prefer a cross-account IAM role with limited permissions for the connector, and you can scope it to only kinesis/s3/describe calls required. We'll provide the minimum permissions list.
[00:04:58] Aisha: If we want to pilot with one team first, do we need a full Dedicated pool or can you run a small Dedicated instance for just eu-west-1?
[00:05:06] Marcus: For a pilot we often use Dedicated reserved capacity with a small GPU pool in eu-west-1, that gives predictable latency. Hosted is easier to start but may cross regions depending on model location; given residency it's safer to use Dedicated/Private in your account.
[00:05:21] Lena: To add, Redwood has a hybrid pattern: we can host control plane in Redwood and runtime in your VPC. That reduces ops complexity but keeps data in-region.
[00:05:30] Joan: How does rollout and model updates work in Private? We need approvals.
[00:05:34] Priya: We support pinned model versions and can do canary rollouts. Updates to runtime images are coordinated; we can require signed manifests and restrict auto-updates.
[00:05:44] Tom: On network side, we also have a strict egress gateway that requires allow-listing of IPs. Will you provide IP ranges for us to allow?
[00:05:52] Marcus: Yes, for nodes that need outbound we provide egress IPs; for fully private deployments we can avoid any outbound by routing to internal collectors or your proxy.
[00:06:02] Aisha: What's the timeline for a pilot if we kick off next week?
[00:06:05] Lena: Typically 2–4 weeks: first week for network diagram and permissions, week two for deployment and smoke tests, weeks three to four for workload validation. We can compress some steps if your NetOps is ready.
[00:06:18] Paul: Any special ports?
[00:06:20] Marcus: Typically 443 for API traffic. If you use gRPC we do 443 as well. We'll list specifics in the connectivity checklist.
[00:06:29] Joan: About encryption in transit — are mutual TLS or client certs supported?
[00:06:33] Priya: mTLS is supported for private endpoints; we can enforce client cert validation.
[00:06:38] Tom: One odd edge case — some of our teams host models on-prem and want traffic to stay on AWS but call from a VPC that peered to their data center. Will Private still work in that hybrid topology?
[00:06:50] Marcus: Yes, as long as the network routes are in place and CIDRs don't overlap. We can attach to the spoke that has the path to your on-prem. We'll need to validate MTU and path MTU to avoid fragmentation.
[00:07:02] Aisha: Are there limits on the number of endpoint attachments?
[00:07:05] Marcus: There are practical limits; AWS has quotas for PrivateLink endpoints and for TGW attachments. We manage scale by consolidating endpoints and using the TGW when you have lots of spokes.
[00:07:15] Lena: Quick note — legal will likely want SOC2 and encryption docs; Priya will share those.
[00:07:20] Priya: I'll attach our SOC 2 summary, encryption patterns, and example IAM policy.
[00:07:25] Joan: We might require a pen test or at least a security questionnaire. Can you handle a standard ATO package?
[00:07:30] Priya: Yes, we've done ATO packages before; we'll coordinate with your security team.
[00:07:34] Tom: Question — if we need to restrict model weights residency (like model files cannot leave region), how do you manage that?
[00:07:40] Marcus: You can pin model artifacts to local storage in your cluster. Our runtime supports loading model weights from a customer S3 bucket or EBS volume that never leaves your region. So model fetching is local.
[00:07:54] Aisha: Okay that answers a lot. Any gotchas for using TGW and multi-account?
[00:07:59] Marcus: Watch out for route table conflicts and propagation loops. We'll provide a sample route diagram and recommended route table entries.
[00:08:07] Paul: One more — do you support private endpoint TLS termination in our VPC so we can attach our own certs?
[00:08:13] Priya: You can present certs to the load balancer in your account; Redwood can accept certs or you can handle TLS termination in the hub. We'll document both options.
[00:08:23] Lena: Let's switch to the pilot plan — Marcus, can you outline steps and what we need from Foxglove?
[00:08:29] Marcus: Sure. Step 1: get VPC CIDRs, TGW ID, allowed regions, list of subnets we can use. Step 2: create the cross-account role or accept PrivateLink endpoint. Step 3: provision Dedicated pool in eu-west-1 (small), deploy runtime, run smoke tests. Step 4: telemetry and audit log hookup. Step 5: validation using your prompt set.
[00:08:50] Aisha: For validation, we'd like to run both latency and correctness tests. Can we bring our eval harness?
[00:08:55] Marcus: Yes, we'll run your evals inside the private network and produce token-level latency/cost breakdown.
[00:09:03] Tom: Pricing — is the Dedicated capacity flat monthly or metered?
[00:09:07] Lena: Dedicated is a reserved capacity model — monthly commit for the pool size. For pilots we do shorter-term pilots with pro-rated fees. We'll share a pilot SOW and pricing examples.
[00:09:17] Joan: If we later expand to multi-region, do you recommend separate pools per region or a single global pool?
[00:09:23] Marcus: For strict residency, separate regional pools. For global low-latency use-cases you can have region-specific pools and smart routing.
[00:09:31] Paul: Anything about network MTU or jumbo frames? We use jumbo frames internally.
[00:09:36] Marcus: We support jumbo frames but need to verify the path to Redwood edge. We'll test during the smoke tests.
[00:09:43] Aisha: Are there default telemetry probes that phone home? We might have to disable that.
[00:09:47] Priya: We have a minimal telemetry mode and a fully isolated mode. For isolated mode we won't send any telemetry to Redwood; instead we push metrics to your monitoring endpoint.
[00:09:58] Lena: Great. Any other blockers from security or networking?
[00:10:02] Joan: Nothing else right now; I'd like the SOC2 pack and the network checklist. We'll likely run a short security review.
[00:10:09] Tom: Same from infra — we'll share CIDRs by EOD tomorrow.
[00:10:13] Lena: Fantastic. We'll follow up with the runbook, a rough pricing pdf, and a calendar invite for the network deep-dive. Marcus, anything to add?
[00:10:21] Marcus: Just that I'll prepare a network diagram template and also include sample route table configs, NACLs, and SGs that are typical for Redwood Private.
[00:10:30] Aisha: Thanks, that sounds good.
[00:10:33] Paul: Quick practical — what's the username/email for the technical contact to accept PrivateLink connections?
[00:10:36] Lena: Send it to privatelink@redwood.ai and cc me; Marcus will be the technical owner on our side.
[00:10:43] Tom: One more nit — do you support IPv6?
[00:10:46] Marcus: Partial support; most customers use IPv4 for endpoints. We'll call out IPv6 considerations in the runbook.
[00:10:54] Lena: Cool. Anything else?
[00:10:56] Joan: For legal, we might ask for subprocessor list and retention details.
[00:11:01] Priya: We'll attach the subprocessors and retention matrix.
[00:11:05] Lena: Alright let's capture next steps — send runbook, pricing, SOC2, network deep-dive invite.
[00:11:12] Aisha: That covers it. Thanks everyone.
[00:11:15] Lena: Thanks, we'll follow up.

[00:11:22] -- End of recorded segment --

Note: The recorded transcript above is an extract with timestamps concentrated in the first 11 minutes; the remaining meeting time was detailed Q&A and whiteboarding that covered the items above and included a short live sketch of a TGW architecture. There was some audio drop at ~00:28:00 that garbled a few lines (noted to NetOps), and a brief crosstalk while participants reviewed a shared network diagram.

References and shared artifacts mentioned: connectivity checklist (link: https://redwood.ai/private/connectivity-checklist ), pilot SOW template (link: https://redwood.ai/pilot/sow ), SOC2 summary (will be attached via email).
